chapters.title: 3.1 COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX

Aggregate functions collapse a set of rows into a single result: how many, how much in total, what's the average, what's the smallest and largest. chapters.customSummary:
- Aggregates collapse many rows into one value; without GROUP BY the query returns a single row for the whole filtered set.
- They power reconciliation of dashboards, reports and exports, plus before/after control totals for migrations (row count, sum, min, max).
- COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts non-NULLs, COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values; choose deliberately.
- All aggregates except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs, so an average may cover fewer rows than expected (e.g., days with a missing punch); confirm the business rule for incomplete rows.
- Empty set: COUNT returns 0 but SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX return NULL (use COALESCE(SUM(x), 0)); also test how the UI shows empty states.
- COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT employee_id) is a quick duplicate smell test.
- SUM of stored totals vs SUM of components (basic + allowances - deductions) reconciles calculations, but offsetting errors can cancel out, so follow up with row-level checks.
- Use DECIMAL for money; SQL Server SUM of INT can overflow (cast to BIGINT).
- Conditional aggregation: SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) gives many tile counts in one query (PostgreSQL also has FILTER).
- AVG: SQL Server truncates integer averages, round with the requirement's rule, and beware the average-of-averages fallacy (8.23 vs 8.25 in our example).
- MIN/MAX work on numbers, dates, times and text; use them as range probes to spot impossible values (future hire dates, 1970 dates, zero or negative days).
- Aggregates are illegal in WHERE (error 1111 / "not allowed in WHERE"); use HAVING.
- Automation: compare tiles with COUNT(*); node-postgres returns COUNT/SUM as strings and mysql2 returns DECIMAL as strings; sum UI money in integer units; match scope (filters, page, soft deletes).
- Don't use table-size estimates as assertions; joins can inflate counts and sums (see Part 4).
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Aggregate functions turn many rows into one value
Up to now, every query returned one output row per input row. Aggregate functions collapse a set of rows into a single result: how many, how much in total, what's the average, what's the smallest and largest. Without a GROUP BY (next chapter), the "set of rows" is everything that survives the WHERE clause, and the query returns exactly one row.
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)              AS total_requests,
       SUM(days)             AS total_days,
```
| ROUND(AVG(days), 2)   AS avg_days, | MIN(days)             AS shortest, |
|---|---|
| MAX(days)             AS longest | FROM   leave_requests; |

total_requests | total_days | avg_days | shortest | longest
9              | 22         | 2.44     | 1        | 6

For a tester these five functions are the vocabulary of reconciliation. Dashboards, reports, exports and summary screens are all aggregates, and the way to verify them is to compute the same aggregate straight from the tables and compare. They're also the basis of the "control totals" (row count, sum, min, max) you take before and after a data migration (6.1, 6.6).
## COUNT has three forms that give different answers
COUNT(*) counts rows, regardless of what's in them. COUNT(column) counts rows where that column is not NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts the unique non-NULL values.
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)                     AS total_rows,
```
| COUNT(manager_id)            AS with_manager, | COUNT(DISTINCT manager_id)   AS distinct_managers, |
|---|---|
| COUNT(DISTINCT department_id) AS departments_used | FROM   employees; |

total_rows | with_manager | distinct_managers | departments_used
5          | 2            | 1                 | 3

Five employees, but only two have a manager, and both report to the same person (employee 1), so there's one distinct manager. Picking the wrong form is one of the most common reasons a "count check" is off. COUNT(1) and COUNT(*) are the same thing, and COUNT(employee_id) equals COUNT(*) only because a primary key can never be NULL. Attendance shows the effect on real data:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)         AS attendance_rows,
       COUNT(check_in)  AS with_check_in,
```
| COUNT(check_out) AS with_check_out, | MIN(check_in)    AS earliest_in, |
|---|---|
| MAX(check_in)    AS latest_in | FROM   attendance; |

## attendance_rows | with_check_in | with_check_out | earliest_in | latest_in
8               | 6             | 6              | 08:55:00    | 09:45:00

Eight rows, but only six have a check-in and six have a check-out, and they aren't the same six (employee 2's 14 Sep row has a check-in but no check-out, employee 3's has the reverse). An equal count doesn't mean the columns match up row by row. The dedicated violation query from 2.3 is what finds the mismatch.
## Every aggregate except COUNT ignores NULLs
SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip NULL values entirely, as if those rows weren't there. That is usually what you want, but it also means an average can quietly be computed over fewer rows than you think. Look at average hours worked:
```sql
SELECT ROUND(AVG(TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in))) / 3600, 2) AS avg_hours,
       COUNT(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in))                             AS days_included
FROM   attendance;
```

avg_hours | days_included
8.25      | 5

Eight attendance rows exist, but TIMEDIFF returns NULL whenever either punch is missing, so only 5 rows contributed. Whether incomplete days should be ignored, counted as zero, or flagged is a business rule. If the requirement says "days without a check-out count as absent," the report and this query disagree by design, and that's worth raising before anyone files a defect. Whenever you verify an average, also ask which rows were left out.
## The empty-set surprise: COUNT gives 0, the rest give NULL
When no rows match, COUNT returns 0 but SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX return NULL, not zero:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(days) AS total_days, AVG(days) AS avg_days, MAX(days) AS longest
FROM   leave_requests
WHERE  status = 'cancelled';
```

n | total_days | avg_days | longest
0 | NULL       | NULL     | NULL

This matters twice. In your own queries, wrap SUM in COALESCE(SUM(days), 0) when you want a zero. And in the app, it's a boundary case worth testing: what does the "Total leave taken" tile show for an employee with no leave, 0, blank, NaN, null, or an error? Empty states are a classic source of front-end bugs.
## SUM: totals, and where they go wrong
SUM adds up numeric values. Two payroll examples show both the use and the trap:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)                     AS payroll_rows,
```
| COUNT(DISTINCT employee_id)  AS employees_paid, | SUM(net_pay)                 AS total_net |
|---|---|
| FROM   payroll | WHERE  pay_month = '2026-08-01'; |

payroll_rows | employees_paid | total_net
4            | 3              | 210500

Four rows for three employees is the giveaway of a duplicate, and the total is inflated by 43,500 as a result (the correct August total is 167,000). If a payroll report displays 210,500, the report is faithfully summing bad data, so the defect is upstream. Comparing COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT employee_id) is a fast duplicate smell test. Chapter 3.2 finds the exact duplicate.
You can also reconcile stored totals against the components that should produce them:
```sql
SELECT SUM(basic_salary + allowances - deductions) AS expected_total,
       SUM(net_pay)                                 AS stored_total,
       SUM(basic_salary + allowances - deductions) - SUM(net_pay) AS difference
FROM   payroll
WHERE  pay_month = '2026-08-01';
```

expected_total | stored_total | difference
211500         | 210500       | 1000

A non-zero difference means something is wrong, and here it's the 1,000 shortfall on employee 3's draft row. But an aggregate check can hide errors. If one row were 1,000 too low and another 1,000 too high, the difference would net to zero and the check would pass. Aggregate checks are quick alarms, not proof. When they pass, follow up with a row-level check (like the WHERE basic + allowances - deductions <> net_pay query from Part 0), and when they fail, drill down to find which rows.
SUM and types deserve a caution. SUM over DECIMAL is exact, and over FLOAT it can drift (1.2). The result type also varies by database: in SQL Server, SUM of an INT column returns an INT and raises an arithmetic overflow error past about 2.1 billion, so you'd write SUM(CAST(amount AS BIGINT)). PostgreSQL and MySQL widen the result type automatically.
## Conditional aggregation with CASE (and FILTER)
Putting a CASE inside an aggregate counts or sums only the rows that meet a condition. It's how you get several "tile" numbers from a single query:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)                                               AS total,
```
| SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'pending'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)   AS pending_cnt, | SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)   AS approved_cnt, |
|---|---|
| SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'approved' THEN days ELSE 0 END) AS approved_days | FROM   leave_requests; |

total | pending_cnt | approved_cnt | approved_days
9     | 3           | 5            | 9

PostgreSQL offers a tidier form, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending'), but the CASE version is the portable one that works on all three databases. Note the ELSE 0: without it, non-matching rows give NULL, and COUNT(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END) still works, but SUM would return NULL on an empty match.
## AVG: the average of what, exactly?
AVG(x) is SUM(x) / COUNT(x), so it's computed over non-NULL values only. Three things go wrong regularly.
First, integer averages can truncate. In SQL Server, AVG of an INT column returns an INT, so the average of 1 and 2 is 1, not 1.5. MySQL and PostgreSQL return decimals. Cast first if you need decimals: AVG(CAST(score AS DECIMAL(10,2))).
Second, rounding. AVG(days) here is 2.4444…, and the app might show 2.4, 2.44 or 2. Always ask what precision and rounding rule the requirement states, and use ROUND(AVG(days), 2) on the same rule (2.4's rounding differences apply).
Third, the average of averages fallacy. Take the attendance hours. Employee 1 has two complete days averaging 8.49 hours, employee 2 has two averaging 8.04, and employee 3 has one averaging 8.17. The average of those three per-employee averages is 8.23, but the average across all five days is 8.25, because employee 3's single day carries less weight in the true average. Both are valid numbers for different questions, and the requirement decides which one the report should show. If a "company average" tile disagrees with your query, check which of the two the app computes.
## MIN and MAX: not just for numbers
MIN and MAX work on any orderable type: numbers, dates, times and text (text follows the column's collation, 2.5). That makes them handy range probes:
```sql
SELECT MIN(hire_date) AS oldest_hire, MAX(hire_date) AS newest_hire FROM employees;
-- 2022-01-20 | 2025-09-01
```

```sql
SELECT MIN(start_date) AS first_leave, MAX(end_date) AS last_leave FROM leave_requests;
-- 2026-05-04 | 2026-12-31
```

```sql
Use them to sniff out impossible data. A MAX(hire_date) in the future, a MIN(work_date) of 1970-01-01 (the classic "zero" timestamp default), or a MIN(days) of 0 or below is a bug signal. They're also a quick way to check the boundaries of a date-range filter: compare the UI's earliest and latest result with MIN and MAX of the filtered set.
```
## Aggregates cannot go in WHERE
WHERE filters individual rows before any aggregation exists, so WHERE COUNT(*) > 2 is illegal:
MySQL:      ERROR 1111 (HY000): Invalid use of group function
## PostgreSQL: ERROR: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE

Filtering on an aggregate's result is the job of HAVING (3.2). If you need "employees whose total is above the average," that's a subquery (5.1).
## Comparing UI numbers with aggregates in automation
A dashboard tile is an aggregate with a friendly label, so this pairing shows up constantly in tests:
```ts
test('Pending Leave tile matches the database', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  const uiValue = Number(await page.getByTestId('pending-leave-count').innerText());   // "3"
```

```ts
  const [rows]: any = await db.execute(
    "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM leave_requests WHERE status = 'pending'");
```

  expect(uiValue).toBe(rows[0].n);   // 3 === 3
});

Two driver gotchas. With node-postgres, COUNT(*) and SUM come back as strings ('3', not 3), because PostgreSQL returns bigint and numeric, so wrap them in Number() or cast in SQL (COUNT(*)::int). With mysql2, DECIMAL values (like sums of money) come back as strings by default, while COUNT returns a number. If an assertion fails with expected 3, received '3', this is why.
To verify a total displayed in a table, read the cells and add them up, but sum in integer units rather than floats:
```ts
const cells = await page.locator('td.net-pay').allInnerTexts();     // ["Rs. 57,500.00", "Rs. 43,500.00", ...]
const uiTotalPaisa = cells
  .map(t => Math.round(Number(t.replace(/[^0-9.]/g, '')) * 100))
  .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
```

Also remember that the table might show only one page of rows while the DB aggregate covers all pages, so match the scope of both sides (same filters, same page, same soft-delete rule) before comparing.
## Speed and estimates
COUNT(*) on a very large table can be slow, since the database may have to scan it. Don't use the table-size "estimates" that clients display (like information_schema.tables.table_rows in MySQL) as assertion values, because they're approximations. Use a real COUNT(*), ideally with a date or ID filter narrowing the scope.
## Where this goes next
The same functions produce the duplicates, mismatched-count and dashboard checks in Part 6, get reused as window functions in 5.5, and reappear in the payroll and leave templates in Part 10. A caution for Part 4: joining tables can multiply rows, which inflates COUNT(*) and SUM without any error. Whenever an aggregate involves a join, sanity-check it against the single-table number.

chapters.title: 3.2 GROUP BY and HAVING
chapters.overviewText: Without GROUP BY, an aggregate summarises the whole table. GROUP BY splits the rows into buckets (one per distinct value of the grouping columns) and computes the aggregate separately for each. You get one output row per bucket. The totals add up (3 + 5 + 1 = 9 requests, 11 + 9 + 2 = 22 days), which is the partition check from 2.1 in aggregate form. You can picture what the engine does: sort the rows into piles by status, then run COUNT and SUM on each pile. In Playwright terms, it's building a Map from status to count by looping over the rows, except the database does it in one step. Many dashboard charts (pie by status, bar by department, line by month) are exactly this query.
chapters.why: 3.2 GROUP BY and HAVING is how a tester proves stored state, not just the screen. Without GROUP BY, an aggregate summarises the whole table.
chapters.when: Open this chapter when you are on the Aggregation path and need GROUP BY and HAVING against the hrms_practice schema, a shared QA database, or a Bizlevate HRMS screen.

practical.scenario: A leave, payroll, attendance, or appointment check depends on GROUP BY and HAVING.
practical.pass: You apply GROUP BY and HAVING on the sample database (or a tagged QA row) and can say what empty vs non-empty results mean.
practical.fail: You copy a blog query, skip GROUP BY and HAVING, or treat a UI success toast as proof the row is correct.

chapters.customSummary:
- GROUP BY makes one bucket per distinct value (or combination) and aggregates each; missing buckets mean zero, so agree on whether the UI/API should show explicit zeros.
- Every non-aggregated SELECT column must be in GROUP BY (MySQL error 1055, PostgreSQL and SQL Server errors); a lax sql_mode can silently return arbitrary values and vary between environments.
- Group by expressions (e.g., month via DATE_FORMAT/TO_CHAR/FORMAT); months with no data don't appear, and leave spanning months is counted by the column you group on, so confirm the rule.
- NULLs form a single group (e.g., employees with no manager).
- WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after; put raw-column conditions in WHERE and aggregate conditions in HAVING, and test >= vs > at the exact boundary (employee 2 with exactly 3 days).
- Duplicate finder: GROUP BY the supposedly-unique columns HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; join or subquery back to fetch the offending rows; missing UNIQUE constraints (payroll) are a design gap to report.
- Compare grouped results with UI/API by loading both into dictionaries and asserting equality (catches missing, extra and wrong buckets).
- Cross-tabs with SUM(CASE ...) per group mirror report grids; row totals should equal the sum of the status columns.
- ROLLUP adds subtotal/grand-total rows (WITH ROLLUP in MySQL, ROLLUP() elsewhere); GROUPING() distinguishes the total row from a real NULL group.
- Top-N with LIMIT 1 hides ties (employees 2 and 3 both have 8 days); add a tiebreaker or use RANK() (5.5), and test tie scenarios in "top" widgets.
- Grouping over joins multiplies rows, so sanity-check against single-table totals and use COUNT(DISTINCT ...) deliberately.
- GROUP BY doesn't guarantee order (MySQL 8 stopped implicit sorting), so add ORDER BY; grouping on expressions can be slow (EXPLAIN, 8.5).
- Attendance summary example separates rows from meaningful days (leave days, missing check-outs), a rule to confirm with the analyst.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## GROUP BY makes one aggregate per bucket
Without GROUP BY, an aggregate summarises the whole table. GROUP BY splits the rows into buckets (one per distinct value of the grouping columns) and computes the aggregate separately for each. You get one output row per bucket.
```sql
SELECT status,
```
| COUNT(*)  AS requests, | SUM(days) AS total_days |
|---|---|
| FROM   leave_requests | GROUP  BY status; |

| status   \| requests \| total_days | pending  \| 3        \| 11 |
|---|---|
| approved \| 5        \| 9 | rejected \| 1        \| 2 |

The totals add up (3 + 5 + 1 = 9 requests, 11 + 9 + 2 = 22 days), which is the partition check from 2.1 in aggregate form. You can picture what the engine does: sort the rows into piles by status, then run COUNT and SUM on each pile. In Playwright terms, it's building a Map from status to count by looping over the rows, except the database does it in one step. Many dashboard charts (pie by status, bar by department, line by month) are exactly this query.

| Grouping by several columns | List more than one column and each combination becomes a bucket: |
|---|---|
| SELECT employee_id, status, COUNT(*) AS requests, SUM(days) AS total_days | FROM   leave_requests |
| GROUP  BY employee_id, status | ORDER  BY employee_id, status; |

| employee_id \| status   \| requests \| total_days | 1           \| approved \| 2        \| 4 | 1           \| pending  \| 1        \| 2 | 2           \| approved \| 2        \| 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2           \| pending  \| 1        \| 3 | 2           \| rejected \| 1        \| 2 | 3           \| approved \| 1        \| 2 | 3           \| pending  \| 1        \| 6 |

Combinations that don't exist (employee 1 has no rejected requests) simply don't appear, so absence of a row means zero. That's a frequent mismatch with UIs and APIs that show an explicit 0 for missing buckets, so decide in advance which behaviour the requirement expects before calling either one a bug.
## The SELECT-list rule
Every column in the SELECT list must either be in the GROUP BY or be wrapped in an aggregate. This query is invalid because the database can't know which of many first_name values to show for each group:
```sql
SELECT department_id, first_name, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
```

MySQL 8:    ERROR 1055 (42000): Expression #2 of SELECT list is not in GROUP BY clause and contains
## nonaggregated column 'hrms_practice.employees.first_name' which is not functionally
            dependent on columns in GROUP BY clause; this is incompatible with sql_mode=only_full_group_by
PostgreSQL: ERROR: column "employees.first_name" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function
SQL Server: Column 'employees.first_name' is invalid in the select list because it is not contained in either
            an aggregate function or the GROUP BY clause.

MySQL enforces this by default since 5.7 (the ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode), but older installations or custom configs may have it off, in which case the query runs and returns an arbitrary first name per group. If you ever see a query that "works" on QA but returns different names on staging, a different sql_mode is a suspect. Exceptions exist: if you group by a table's primary key, MySQL and PostgreSQL allow the other columns from that table, because they're functionally determined by the key.
## Grouping by expressions, including months
You can group by a computed value. A leave-per-month breakdown is a typical report:
```sql
-- MySQL
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(start_date, '%Y-%m') AS ym,
```
| COUNT(*)  AS requests, | SUM(days) AS total_days | FROM   leave_requests |
|---|---|---|
| GROUP  BY DATE_FORMAT(start_date, '%Y-%m') | ORDER  BY ym; | -- PostgreSQL: TO_CHAR(start_date, 'YYYY-MM')   SQL Server: FORMAT(start_date, 'yyyy-MM') |

| ym      \| requests \| total_days | 2026-05 \| 1        \| 2 | 2026-06 \| 1        \| 2 | 2026-07 \| 2        \| 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08 \| 1        \| 2 | 2026-09 \| 1        \| 1 | 2026-10 \| 2        \| 5 | 2026-12 \| 1        \| 6 |

Three things to notice. November is missing, because months with no data produce no bucket, so a chart that should show a zero bar for November needs a calendar table joined in (a LEFT JOIN, 4.1), and that's a good test scenario for any month-by-month chart. The request starting 31 Aug and ending 1 Sep is counted only in August, since we grouped by start_date. Whether a leave spanning two months should be split, counted in the first month, or counted in both is a business rule to confirm. And repeating the full expression in GROUP BY is portable: MySQL and PostgreSQL also accept the alias (GROUP BY ym), but SQL Server doesn't.
## NULL forms its own group
All NULLs in a grouping column land in one bucket, unlike WHERE comparisons where NULL never equals anything:
```sql
SELECT manager_id, COUNT(*) AS employees FROM employees GROUP BY manager_id;
```

manager_id | employees
NULL       | 3
1          | 2

The NULL row is easy to misread as "no data." It means "employees with no manager." UIs sometimes drop that bucket or label it "Unknown" or "N/A", so check how yours handles it.
## WHERE versus HAVING
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation, so it's the only place you can filter on an aggregate result. This follows the logical order from Part 1 (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY).
-- Employees with more than 2 leave requests
```sql
SELECT employee_id, COUNT(*) AS requests
FROM   leave_requests
GROUP  BY employee_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
```

employee_id | requests
1           | 3
2           | 4

Combining both, as in "approved leave only, and only employees with at least 3 approved days":
```sql
SELECT employee_id, COUNT(*) AS approved_requests, SUM(days) AS approved_days
FROM   leave_requests
WHERE  status = 'approved'          -- row filter, runs first
GROUP  BY employee_id
HAVING SUM(days) >= 3;              -- group filter, runs after aggregation
```

employee_id | approved_requests | approved_days
1           | 2                 | 4
2           | 2                 | 3

Employee 2 has exactly 3 approved days and is included, which is the boundary case (>= versus >) to test against the app's "3 or more days needs a document" style of rule. Employee 3 has 2 and is excluded.
A rule of thumb: put conditions on raw columns in WHERE and conditions on aggregates in HAVING. MySQL lets you put a plain column condition in HAVING, but it makes the database group everything first and filter later, which is slower and hides your intent. Also, MySQL allows aliases inside HAVING, while PostgreSQL and SQL Server don't, so repeat the aggregate expression if you want portable code.
## The duplicate-finder pattern
GROUP BY on the columns that should be unique, plus HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, finds duplicates. It is probably the single most useful query pattern in this manual:
```sql
SELECT employee_id, pay_month, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM   payroll
GROUP  BY employee_id, pay_month
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

employee_id | pay_month  | copies
2           | 2026-08-01 | 2

That pinpoints the duplicate that inflated the August total in 3.1. To see the rows involved (which you'll need for a bug report), join the result back or use a subquery (5.1):
```sql
SELECT p.*
FROM   payroll p
WHERE  (p.employee_id, p.pay_month) IN (
         SELECT employee_id, pay_month FROM payroll
         GROUP BY employee_id, pay_month HAVING COUNT(*) > 1);
```

Two testing observations follow. First, the payroll table has no UNIQUE (employee_id, pay_month) constraint, and that's why the duplicate got in. It's worth reporting as a design gap even after cleaning the row (8.1). The attendance table does have that kind of constraint on (employee_id, work_date), so duplicate rows can't exist there, but you should still test the app's behaviour for a double check-in, expecting a clean error message rather than a raw database error. Second, be careful defining "duplicate." Two payroll rows for the same employee and month are wrong, but two leave requests for the same dates might be legitimate re-applications after a rejection. The grouping columns encode the business definition.
## Grouping to compare with the UI or API
Because a chart or summary is just a GROUP BY, you can compare the two structures directly. A pytest example that checks a leave summary endpoint against the database:
```py
def test_leave_summary_by_status_matches_db(api, db):
    resp = api.get("/api/leave/summary", params={"year": 2026}).json()
    api_counts = {row["status"]: row["count"] for row in resp["byStatus"]}
```

    db.execute("""
| SELECT status, COUNT(*) | FROM   leave_requests |
|---|---|
| WHERE  start_date >= '2026-01-01' AND start_date < '2027-01-01' | GROUP  BY status |
| """) | db_counts = {status: n for status, n in db.fetchall()} |

## assert api_counts == db_counts    # {'pending': 3, 'approved': 5, 'rejected': 1}

Comparing whole dictionaries catches a missing bucket, an extra bucket and a wrong count in one assertion. If your API returns zero-count buckets (say "cancelled": 0) while the database query doesn't, the assertion fails for a reason that isn't a defect, so agree on the convention first, or add the missing keys to the DB result before comparing.
The same idea works in Playwright by reading the labels and values of a chart's legend or tooltip data into an object and comparing it with the query result.
## Cross-tabs (pivots) with conditional aggregation
GROUP BY produces "long" output, one row per bucket. Reports often want a "wide" grid, where each status is its own column. Combine GROUP BY with the SUM(CASE ...) idea from 3.1:
```sql
SELECT employee_id,
```
| SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'pending'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending, | SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS approved, | SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'rejected' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS rejected, |
|---|---|---|
| COUNT(*)                                             AS total | FROM   leave_requests | GROUP  BY employee_id; |

| employee_id \| pending \| approved \| rejected \| total | 1           \| 1       \| 2        \| 0        \| 3 |
|---|---|
| 2           \| 1       \| 2        \| 1        \| 4 | 3           \| 1       \| 1        \| 0        \| 2 |

This shape maps neatly onto a table in the UI (one row per employee, one column per status), so it's a good expected-value source for table-based report tests. A quick consistency check is that each row's three status columns must add up to total; if they don't, some rows have a status outside the expected list.
## Grand totals with ROLLUP
ROLLUP adds subtotal and grand-total rows to a grouped result, so one query gives you both the breakdown and the number the "Total" line on a report should show:
```sql
-- MySQL
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS requests, SUM(days) AS total_days
FROM   leave_requests
GROUP  BY status WITH ROLLUP;
```

```sql
-- PostgreSQL / SQL Server
-- GROUP BY ROLLUP (status)
```

status   | requests | total_days
| approved \| 5        \| 9 | pending  \| 3        \| 11 |
|---|---|
| rejected \| 1        \| 2 | NULL     \| 9        \| 22        ← the grand total row |

The NULL in the last row means "all statuses," which is confusing when a real NULL group might also exist. The GROUPING(status) function (available in all three) returns 1 for the rollup row and 0 for a real group, and lets you tell them apart. This is a neat way to check that a report's footer total equals the sum of its rows.
Top-N per group, and the ties trap
"Who has taken the most leave?" looks like a GROUP BY plus LIMIT 1:
```sql
SELECT employee_id, SUM(days) AS total_days
```
| FROM   leave_requests | GROUP  BY employee_id |
|---|---|
| ORDER  BY total_days DESC | LIMIT  1; |

Employee 2 and employee 3 both have 8 days (employee 1 has 6), so LIMIT 1 returns one of the two and silently hides the other. Which one it returns can even change between runs. Adding a tiebreaker (, employee_id) makes the result stable, but the honest answer is "a tie." For "top N including ties," you need a ranking function (RANK(), chapter 5.5). When a report or dashboard shows a "Top performer" or "Most absent" style widget, the tie is a great test scenario: make two people equal and see what the UI does.
## Grouping and joins: the inflation problem
Everything here has used a single table. Once you group over a join (Part 4), each row on the "one" side is repeated once per matching row on the "many" side, and COUNT(*) or SUM then count the repeats. For example, joining employees to leave requests and then counting employees per department would count each employee once per leave request. The habit that protects you is to compare a grouped result against a simple single-table number (total employees, total days), and to use COUNT(DISTINCT ...) deliberately. We return to this in 4.1 and 6.3.
## Group order and performance notes
GROUP BY doesn't guarantee output order. MySQL before 8.0 often sorted the groups as a side effect and 8.0 stopped doing so, so a test that passed before an upgrade can start failing. Add ORDER BY whenever the order matters. On big tables, grouping and HAVING can be expensive, and grouping by an expression such as DATE_FORMAT(...) can't use an index, so a slow report is worth EXPLAIN (8.5).
## A worked example: attendance summary per employee
Here is a typical "expected values for a report" query, drawing on 3.1 and 3.2 together:
```sql
SELECT employee_id,
       COUNT(*)                                                              AS punch_rows,
       COUNT(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in))                                  AS complete_days,
       ROUND(AVG(TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in))) / 3600, 2)      AS avg_hours,
       SUM(CASE WHEN check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS missing_checkout
FROM   attendance
GROUP  BY employee_id;
```

| employee_id \| punch_rows \| complete_days \| avg_hours \| missing_checkout | 1           \| 3          \| 2             \| 8.49      \| 0 |
|---|---|
| 2           \| 3          \| 2             \| 8.04      \| 1 | 3           \| 2          \| 1             \| 8.17      \| 0 |

Employee 1's third row (15 Sep) has no punches at all because it was an approved leave day, so it counts as a row but not as a complete day, and it isn't a "missing checkout" either. That difference between rows and meaningful days is exactly the sort of rule a tester must pin down with the analyst before deciding whether an attendance report is correct. Chapter 10.3 turns queries like this into reusable templates.
